extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent attorneys, and litigators (UK / common-law jurisdictions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for assessing novelty, inventorship, and the effect of prior/public use on the validity of patents, illustrated by case law. Focuses on who is the true inventor, contributions of assistants/servants, and what counts as prior/public use or disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent simultaneous discovery does not defeat patent unless public
rubrics_metrics.description: If one discovers and can produce an effect from his own experiments, judgment, and skill, it is no objection that someone else has made a similar discovery in his mind unless it has become public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee is not deprived of benefit merely because another had also invented it, unless that other had brought it into public use. Private, uncommunicated discovery (even if earlier) does not prevent another from obtaining a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint inventors must all apply
rubrics_metrics.description: When an invention results from the combined operation of two or more minds, it is necessary that all the inventors should apply for the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents have been defeated where a patentee owed a material part of the invention to another person and satisfactory evidence established that fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assistants/workmen's mere manual labour does not negate inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The suggestions and aid of workmen employed by the inventor to carry out his ideas will have no such effect (i.e., will not defeat the inventor's claim) provided the substantial part and leading idea, the principle of an invention, belong to one person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventor may properly call in assistance to work out and improve his original conception and still procure a patent. Whether a workman was a mere 'machine' carrying out directions or the true inventor is a question of fact for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where the workman suggested the principle he may be inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: If a workman suggested the principle to the person who appears as patentee, then the workman would be the inventor; conversely, if the patentee suggested the principle and the workman assisted in carrying it into effect, the patentee is the true inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination depends on evidence of who suggested the leading idea versus who executed it; jury should judge probabilities. Compensation or failure to take out a patent by the true originator is relevant evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent/servant discoveries in course of employment belong to employer
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a person employed by a firm in their laboratory (an agent/servant) makes a discovery in the course of that employment, the benefit of the discovery belongs to the employers, who may apply for the patent in their own names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If many stages of the discovery were due to the employee but done with employer's materials, assistance and in their lab, the employer can be justified in applying for the patent (Kurtz v. Spence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere employment of inventor does not automatically make employer the inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: But where the patentee has no closer connection with the invention than that of being simply the employer of the inventor, he will not be able to sustain his patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the true source of the invention can be traced to someone else (even an employee), the patentee's claim may fail (Arkwright; Barker v. Shaw). Ownership depends on substance of relationship and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate improvements by assistants may be embodied by original inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person discovers an improved principle and employs engineers, agents or other persons to assist him, and they in the course of experiments make valuable discoveries accessory to the main principle, such improvements are the property of the inventor of the original improved principle and may be embodied in his patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each case depends on merits; when the principle and object of an invention are complete without a suggested improvement, a workman's suggestion of a mode to carry it into effect should not render the patent void (Allen v. Raicson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public use (or public exercise) invalidates patent
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention was, at the time the letters patent were granted, in any degree of general use or was known to the world publicly and practised openly so that any other person might have the means of acquiring the knowledge of it, then the letters patent are void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public use means the use is not secret but public — e.g., putting a lock on one's gate and using it for years is public use. Whether a use is 'public' is a question of fact for the jury; extensive case examples (Tennant; Carpenter v. Smith; Cornish v. Keene).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private experiments and non-communicated trials do not amount to public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments made in private, never communicated to the world and laid by, are not public use and will not defeat a subsequently filed patent by another who obtains the grant first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence classifies previous acts as mere experiments or unsuccessful trials kept secret, that will be no answer to validity of the later patent. The line between experiment and public use depends on particular facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited manufacture/sale or use by few can nonetheless be 'public use'
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of an article by half-a-dozen individuals, or even one, in a public manner such that any person having access might acquire knowledge of it, can constitute public use and destroy novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selling or manufacturing and selling several dozens, or placing articles where the public can observe or access them, has been held to be sufficient public use (Freer/Tilsley example; Losh v. Hague).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication by specimens/materials that enable reproduction counts as disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: If material or specimens are in public use or circulation and are such that a person of ordinary competence could reproduce the process or article from them, that is substantially a publication of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign-manufactured articles shown or sold in the country which reveal the means of manufacture can anticipate a later patent (Hancock v. Goodyear; jury must assess whether the material disclosed the invention in substance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale in England of articles made abroad anticipates a later patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale in England of articles made abroad is an anticipation of a subsequently patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Importation and placing the finished articles on the English market can amount to public user/disclosure sufficient to invalidate a later English patent (Jensen v. Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior user in a colony does not affect UK patent validity
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior user of an invention in a colony does not affect the validity of a patent subsequently obtained for the same invention in the United Kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a principle established in case law (House of Lords reference) — territorial limits of prior user matter for UK patents (see cited case Holler v. ...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior user need be proved clearly; discontinuance does not necessarily save the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: To break down a patent on the ground of prior public user the fact of anticipation must be very clearly made out. It is not necessary to show that the user continued up to the date of the patent being granted; even discontinued prior use may invalidate a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have left open some questions about very remote discontinued uses, but generally prior public use (even if stopped before grant) can render the patent invalid (Househill Co. v. Neilson and other cases). Burden of proof on defendant relying on prior user.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior existence of similar material does not defeat patent absent application to claimed purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing that sheets or materials of a certain composition had been previously made does not destroy a patent unless it can be shown that the hidden virtue or quality had been ascertained and applied to the same useful purpose claimed by the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence must show that the earlier production amounted to an application of the material to the useful purpose for which the patent was taken out; mere coincidence of components or proportions in ordinary manufacture is insufficient (Muntz example).
